Discover how spending time in nature may encourage healthier eating through improved body appreciation, self-compassion and intuitive eating.


## Introduction


Spending time outdoors may offer more benefits than simply helping us relax and unwind. New research suggests that connecting with nature could also be associated with healthier eating habits by encouraging people to develop a more positive relationship with their bodies.


A study led by Anglia Ruskin University (ARU) explored the relationship between time spent in natural environments, body appreciation, self-compassion and intuitive eating. The findings suggest that people who feel more connected to nature may also find it easier to approach food and eating in a healthier, more balanced way.


Although more research is needed, the results highlight an interesting connection between our surroundings and our overall wellbeing.


## What Does the Research Say About Nature and Healthy Eating?


The research, published in the journal *Body Image* , involved 500 participants who answered questions about their everyday experiences with nature.


Participants also completed questionnaires measuring their body image, levels of self-compassion and connection with the natural world. Researchers then examined how these factors related to intuitive eating, an approach that encourages individuals to pay attention to their body's natural hunger and fullness signals.


The study found that the direct relationship between exposure to nature and intuitive eating was not statistically significant. However, the researchers identified indirect associations involving body appreciation and self-compassion.


In other words, spending time in nature may be connected to healthier eating behaviours through the way people perceive themselves and respond to their own needs.


Professor Viren Swami, a social psychology professor at Anglia Ruskin University, said the findings offer initial evidence of possible pathways linking contact with nature and eating habits.


The results are promising, but they do not prove that spending time outdoors directly causes people to make healthier food choices.


## 1. Nature May Help Improve Body Appreciation


Body appreciation means recognising and respecting your body, rather than focusing exclusively on its appearance or perceived imperfections.


Modern lifestyles can expose people to unrealistic beauty standards, social comparisons and pressure to achieve a particular body shape. These influences may affect confidence and contribute to negative feelings about food and eating.


Natural environments can provide an opportunity to step away from these pressures. A walk through a park, time in a garden or a visit to the countryside may encourage people to focus on how their bodies feel and what they can do, rather than how they look.


Developing a more accepting attitude towards the body may also help reduce the urge to follow restrictive eating rules purely for appearance-related reasons.


However, nature is not a treatment for body image difficulties, and individual experiences will vary. Its potential value lies in providing an accessible setting for relaxation, reflection and a greater appreciation of everyday life.


## 2. Self-Compassion Could Influence Food Choices


Self-compassion involves treating yourself with understanding and kindness, particularly when things do not go according to plan.


When it comes to eating, this may mean avoiding harsh self-criticism after enjoying a favourite dessert or having a meal that does not match your usual routine.


People who approach themselves with greater compassion may be better able to move away from guilt-driven food decisions and focus on their longer-term wellbeing.


Spending time in green spaces may provide an opportunity to slow down, manage everyday stress and practise a kinder attitude towards oneself. The study suggests that self-compassion could be one factor connecting nature exposure with intuitive eating.


It is important to remember that the research identified associations rather than proving a cause-and-effect relationship. Further studies are needed to understand how these psychological factors interact over time.


## 3. Understanding Intuitive Eating


Intuitive eating is an approach to food that encourages people to recognise and respond to their body's internal signals instead of relying entirely on rigid dietary rules.


It involves paying attention to hunger, noticing when you feel comfortably full, enjoying food without unnecessary guilt and recognising the influence of emotions on eating behaviour.


For example, someone practising intuitive eating might pause before a meal to assess their hunger or notice whether they are eating because they feel physically hungry, stressed or bored.


The approach does not mean ignoring nutrition or avoiding all structure. Rather, it aims to support a more flexible relationship with food that considers physical needs, satisfaction and personal preferences.


The findings from Anglia Ruskin University suggest that body appreciation and self-compassion may be relevant to this approach. Nevertheless, the study does not establish that spending more time outdoors will automatically lead to intuitive eating.


## 4. How to Incorporate More Nature Into Your Daily Routine


You do not need to live near mountains, forests or the coast to enjoy the potential benefits of spending time outdoors. Small, consistent changes can help you connect with your surroundings.


Here are some simple ideas:


- **Take a daily walk:** Spend 10 to 20 minutes walking through a local park, garden or tree-lined street when practical.
- **Eat outdoors occasionally:** Enjoy lunch in a garden or park when the weather and circumstances allow.
- **Try gardening:** Growing herbs, vegetables or flowers can provide a hands-on way to connect with nature.
- **Take mindful breaks:** Notice the sounds, colours and textures around you instead of focusing entirely on your phone.
- **Explore local green spaces:** Visit nearby parks, nature trails or community gardens when you have time.
- **Combine movement with relaxation:** Choose outdoor activities you enjoy, such as gentle walking, birdwatching or sitting beneath a tree.


These activities should be enjoyable rather than another source of pressure. Even brief contact with outdoor environments may offer a welcome break from a busy routine, although the ideal duration and frequency for supporting eating behaviours remain unclear.


## 5. Healthy Eating Still Depends on Several Factors


While the relationship between nature and eating habits is worth exploring, nutrition is influenced by many factors, including food availability, income, culture, health, personal preferences and time constraints.


A balanced eating pattern generally includes a variety of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, protein sources and other foods that meet individual nutritional needs.


Foods such as berries, leafy greens, nuts, seeds and oily fish can provide important nutrients, including vitamins, minerals, fibre and healthy fats. However, no single food can guarantee better mental or physical health, and the term "superfood" should not be interpreted as a medical or nutritional guarantee.


Sleep, physical activity, stress management and access to suitable food can also contribute to overall wellbeing.


Spending time in nature may complement these habits, but it should not be presented as a substitute for balanced nutrition, appropriate healthcare or professional support when needed.


## 6. What Are the Limitations of the Study?


Although the findings offer an interesting perspective, several limitations should be considered.


First, the research relied on self-reported questionnaires. Participants' answers may not always reflect their behaviour accurately and can be influenced by memory or personal interpretation.


Second, the study identified associations rather than demonstrating that nature exposure directly changes eating behaviour.


Further research involving participants from different countries and backgrounds could help establish whether the findings apply more widely. Long-term studies and research examining actual eating behaviours may also help clarify the relationship.


These limitations mean the results should be viewed as an early step towards understanding how environmental and psychological factors may work together to influence food choices.


## Conclusion


The connection between nature and healthy eating habits offers an encouraging reminder that wellbeing involves more than the food on our plates.


Research from Anglia Ruskin University suggests that spending time in natural environments may be indirectly associated with intuitive eating through greater body appreciation and self-compassion. While the findings do not prove that nature causes healthier eating, they provide a useful starting point for further investigation.


Taking a walk, tending a garden or spending a few quiet moments outdoors can be simple ways to make nature part of everyday life. Combined with balanced nutrition and a supportive attitude towards your body, these activities may contribute to a healthier approach to overall wellbeing.


Rather than viewing outdoor time as a quick fix, consider it one small part of a broader lifestyle that supports physical and mental health.

This article is for general informational and educational purposes only. It is not intended to replace professional medical advice, diagnosis or treatment. The research discussed identifies associations and does not establish that spending time in nature directly causes healthier eating habits. Individual nutritional needs and health circumstances vary.
